title: Training loss becomes NaN at step 4,000
situation: A transformer trains fine, then loss spikes and turns NaN. Same code worked at a smaller scale.

steps.label: Locate
items: Reproduce deterministically (fixed seed, same batch order) and log grad-norm, loss scale and max-abs activations per layer; find the first step with inf/NaN.
Check the batch at that step for bad data (empty target, huge values, NaN in features).

steps.label: Likely math causes
items: Overflow in softmax/exp without log-sum-exp; log(0) in a custom loss; division by a tiny variance (epsilon too small in fp16).
LR too high for the Hessian's largest eigenvalue (stability needs eta < 2/lambda_max): add warmup, lower LR.
fp16 underflow/overflow: use bf16 or dynamic loss scaling; keep norms/softmax in fp32.

steps.label: Fix
items: Gradient clipping (global norm), warmup, AdamW eps 1e-8 to 1e-6, pre-LN, QK-norm for attention logit growth.
Add a non-finite check that skips the step and logs the batch; gradient-check custom ops in float64.

followups.q: How do you know clipping is hiding a real bug?
followups.a: If clipping is active on most steps, the effective LR is lower than configured and the instability is still there. Track the fraction of clipped steps; fix the root cause (LR, init, data) until it is rare.

title: Reviewer: 'your +0.4% gain is within noise'
situation: Your journal submission got a major revision. The main table has single-run numbers and the improvement is small.

steps.label: Quantify
items: Run >=5-10 seeds for your method and every baseline with identical data order policy; report mean +- std and a 95% CI of the paired difference.
Do a power analysis: n ~ 2((1.96+0.84) sigma / delta)^2; if you cannot reach it, say the effect is not established.

steps.label: Strengthen
items: Paired bootstrap over test items; Wilcoxon/Friedman across datasets; Holm correction for many comparisons.
Re-tune baselines with the same search budget; add ablations that remove each component.

steps.label: Respond
items: Point-by-point rebuttal: quote the comment, state the new experiment, show the table/figure, and soften any claim the data does not support.

followups.q: What if after more seeds the effect disappears?
followups.a: Report it honestly: reframe the paper around analysis, efficiency (same accuracy, lower cost) or negative results. A smaller true claim is publishable; a false one is not.

title: Train accuracy 99%, validation 71%
situation: A model on a small dataset generalizes badly.

steps.label: Diagnose
items: Check leakage first (duplicates, shared users, time order); an inflated validation score is a worse problem than a low one.
Plot learning curves vs data size: high variance (large gap) or high bias (both low)?

steps.label: Act
items: High variance: more data/augmentation, weight decay, dropout, early stopping, smaller or pre-trained model, ensembling.
High bias: bigger model, better features, longer training, lower regularization.

followups.q: Does double descent change this advice?
followups.a: It means test error can fall again beyond the interpolation threshold, so a larger model may help even when it fits the training set exactly - but verify empirically with a clean validation protocol.

title: Which generative model for a new paper?
situation: You must generate realistic medical images from few examples and publish the result in an IEEE journal.

steps.label: Choose
items: Diffusion (conditional or latent) for quality/coverage; a VAE if you need a tractable latent and speed; avoid raw GANs unless you can handle instability and mode collapse.
Few data: fine-tune a pre-trained model with LoRA; consider augmentation and a strong prior.

steps.label: Evaluate
items: FID plus precision/recall, nearest-neighbour memorization check, downstream task utility, clinician review.
Statistics over seeds, ablation of conditioning/guidance, privacy and ethics section.

followups.q: How do you show the model is not memorizing patients?
followups.a: Nearest-neighbour search in a feature space against the training set, membership-inference attack tests, and a held-out-patient evaluation.
